entries.title: Pablo Picasso on the Act of Creation
entries.body_text: The purpose of art is washing the dust of daily life off our souls.

entries.title: Gustave Courbet and the Birth of Realism
entries.body_text: On June 10, 1819, Gustave Courbet was born in Ornans, France. Rejecting the Romantic idealization of his contemporaries, Courbet insisted on painting only what he could see and know directly. His monumental canvas 'The Stone Breakers' (1849) depicted common laborers with a gravity previously reserved for mythological heroes, scandalizing the Paris Salon. Courbet later organized a private 'Pavilion of Realism' in 1855 to exhibit his rejected works on his own terms—an act of artistic defiance that prefigured the independent exhibition movements that followed.
entries.image_alt_text: The Stone Breakers by Gustave Courbet, 1849, oil on canvas, formerly Gemäldegalerie Alte Meister, Dresden (destroyed 1945)
entries.rights_note: Public domain. Gustave Courbet died December 31, 1877; work created 1849. Image sourced from Wikimedia Commons.

entries.title: Frida Kahlo on Painting Her Reality
entries.body_text: I never painted dreams. I painted my own reality.

entries.title: The First Impressionist Exhibition, 1874
entries.body_text: On April 15, 1874, a group of French artists including Claude Monet, Edgar Degas, Camille Pissarro, Berthe Morisot, and Pierre-Auguste Renoir opened an independent exhibition at the studio of photographer Nadar in Paris. Dismissed by critics—one derided Monet's 'Impression, Sunrise' (1872) as a mere 'impression'—the show nonetheless changed art history permanently. The eight Impressionist exhibitions held between 1874 and 1886 dismantled the stranglehold of the Paris Salon and established the model of the independent artist-organized show.
entries.image_alt_text: Impression, Sunrise by Claude Monet, 1872, oil on canvas, 48 x 63 cm, Musée Marmottan Monet, Paris
entries.rights_note: Public domain. Claude Monet died December 5, 1926; work created 1872. Image sourced from Wikimedia Commons.

entries.title: Edward Hopper: Painter of American Solitude
entries.body_text: Edward Hopper was born on July 22, 1882, in Nyack, New York. Trained under Robert Henri in New York, Hopper developed a uniquely American visual language built on sharp light, geometric architecture, and human figures caught in moments of quiet isolation. His 1942 painting 'Nighthawks'—depicting three customers and a counter attendant in a late-night diner—became an enduring icon of urban loneliness and the alienation of modern life. Hopper once said the diner was 'unconsciously a painting of loneliness,' though he disputed that interpretation publicly.
entries.image_alt_text: Nighthawks by Edward Hopper, 1942, oil on canvas, 84.1 x 152.4 cm, Art Institute of Chicago
entries.rights_note: Public domain in the United States. Edward Hopper died May 15, 1967; 'Nighthawks' (1942) was published before 1978 without copyright renewal. Open access image courtesy of the Art Institute of Chicago via Wikimedia Commons.

entries.body_text: A drawing is simply a line going for a walk.

entries.title: The Birth of Paul Delaroche, Master of Historical Drama
entries.body_text: Paul Delaroche was born on July 17, 1797, in Paris. Known for his meticulously staged historical scenes, Delaroche brought theatrical intensity to academic painting during the 19th century. His masterpiece 'The Execution of Lady Jane Grey' (1833) exemplifies his ability to blend emotional storytelling with precise draftsmanship, capturing the tragic fate of England's 'Nine Days' Queen' with haunting clarity. Delaroche's work bridged the gap between Neoclassicism and emerging Romantic sensibilities, influencing generations of painters who sought to merge narrative power with visual realism.

entries.title: The Death of Édouard Manet, Father of Modernism
entries.body_text: Édouard Manet died on April 30, 1883, leaving behind a body of work that helped redefine the trajectory of Western art. Rejecting academic conventions, Manet embraced contemporary subjects and bold brushwork that shocked the Paris Salon but inspired the next generation of Impressionists. His late masterpiece 'A Bar at the Folies-Bergère' (1882) exemplifies his fascination with modern urban life and complex spatial ambiguity. Manet's innovations laid the groundwork for modernism, bridging Realism and the radical experimentation that followed.

entries.rights_note: Public domain. Édouard Manet died 1883; work created 1882. Image sourced from Wikimedia Commons.

entries.body_text: Nothing makes me happier than to contemplate nature and then go and paint it.

entries.title: The Birth of Frédéric Bazille, Early Impressionist Innovator
entries.body_text: Frédéric Bazille was born on December 6, 1841, in Montpellier, France. A close friend of Monet, Renoir, and Sisley, Bazille played a pivotal role in the early development of Impressionism before his life was cut short in the Franco-Prussian War. His painting 'La Robinsonade' (1865) reveals his interest in natural light, outdoor settings, and the relaxed informality that would later define the movement. Though his career was brief, Bazille's contributions helped shape the foundations of Impressionist painting.
entries.image_alt_text: La Robinsonade by Frédéric Bazille, 1865, oil on canvas, public domain
entries.rights_note: Public domain. Frédéric Bazille died 1870; work created 1865. Image sourced from Wikimedia Commons.
